title: The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program: Paid Remote Fellowship for Science Journalists Worldwide
summary: The Open Notebook (TON) offers a paid, remote, part-time fellowship program for early-career science journalists who want to strengthen their reporting, interviewing, writing, and storytelling skills while gaining practical experience in professional science journalism. During the year-long fellowship, participants work closely with experienced science-journalism mentors to develop story ideas, report and write articles for publication at The Open Notebook , receive editorial guidance, and become part of TON s wider editorial and fellowship community. For the 2026 fellowship period described by The Open Notebook, the program ran for 12 months , was conducted remotely and part-time, and offered a $6,600 stipend . The scheduled start date was February 23, 2026 . However, prospective applicants should pay close attention to the application status. Applications for the 2026 fellowship period are now closed. The Open Notebook states that it expects applications for the 2027 fellowship to open by late September 2026. Applicants interested in the next cycle should therefore monitor The Open Notebook for the announcement of the 2027 application deadline. This detailed guide explains how The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship works, what fellows do, the expected time commitment, eligibility requirements, selection criteria, application materials, and other important information prospective applicants should understand. About The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program The Open Notebook s Early-Career Fellowship is designed to help emerging science journalists develop professionally through practical reporting, writing, editing, mentoring, and participation in an established science-journalism community. Rather than functioning solely as a classroom-style training program, the fellowship places participants in a real editorial environment. Fellows work with mentors to plan, report, write, revise, and prepare articles for publication by The Open Notebook. The program lasts for one year and is conducted remotely on a part-time basis. The fellowship is supported by the Burroughs Wellcome Fund , which The Open Notebook says has supported the program since 2013. For journalists at an early stage of their careers, this structure provides an opportunity to develop their craft while building published work and professional relationships within the science-journalism community. The Open Notebook Fellowship at a Glance The key details provided for the 2026 fellowship cycle were: Program duration: 12 months Working arrangement: Part-time Location: Remote 2026 fellowship start date: February 23, 2026 Stipend: $6,600 2026 application deadline: October 31, 2025 Current application status: Closed Expected opening of 2027 applications: By late September 2026 Applicants should understand that October 31, 2025 is not the deadline for the upcoming 2027 fellowship . It was the deadline for applications to the 2026 fellowship period. The deadline for the 2027 cycle was not provided in the supplied information. What Fellows Do During the Program The fellowship centers on practical journalism. During the remote, part-time program, fellows pitch, report, and write articles intended for publication by The Open Notebook. The work includes a mixture of story behind the story interviews and reported features , allowing fellows to explore how journalism is produced while simultaneously improving their own reporting and writing skills. An important part of the program is the relationship between each fellow and an experienced science journalist serving as a mentor. One-on-One Mentorship Fellows have weekly phone or video meetings with their mentors . Mentors help fellows: Develop and refine potential story ideas; Shape stories into workable projects; Improve reporting techniques; Strengthen writing; Review and edit article drafts; Navigate the reporting and revision process; Develop their understanding of the craft of science journalism; and Think about broader professional and career-development questions. The mentoring component therefore extends beyond correcting individual articles. It is designed to help fellows become stronger journalists and make more informed decisions as they develop their careers. Become Part of The Open Notebook Editorial Community The fellowship also provides a community element. Fellows and mentors participate in a Slack discussion group that includes current and former fellowship participants as well as editors from The Open Notebook. Fellows participate in cohort-based activities through this Slack community during the fellowship. Importantly, membership in the community continues after the fellowship ends . This can be particularly valuable for early-career journalists because professional development often depends not only on technical skills but also on access to peers, experienced journalists, editors, feedback, and professional relationships. How Much Work Does the Fellowship Require? Although the fellowship is part-time, applicants should not assume that the workload is minimal. The Open Notebook estimates that most fellows spend approximately five to seven hours per week on average completing fellowship-related responsibilities. However, this is an estimate rather than a fixed weekly workload. The amount of time required can vary depending on: A fellow s previous journalism experience; Individual working and writing style; The complexity of a particular article; Whether the fellow is researching, reporting, writing, revising, or fact-checking at a particular point in the process; and The number and complexity of revisions required. Some weeks may consequently require more than five to seven hours, while others may require less. Fellows Are Expected to Produce Four Major Articles A major component of the fellowship is producing four articles of approximately 1,500 to 2,000 words each for The Open Notebook. Producing these stories involves considerably more than simply drafting four pieces. Fellows are expected to participate in the broader reporting and editorial process, which may include: Developing story ideas; Researching proposed subjects; Conducting interviews; Reporting stories; Writing drafts; Receiving editorial feedback; Completing multiple rounds of revisions; Annotating stories for fact-checking; Meeting article deadlines; and Preparing work for eventual publication. The program therefore requires sustained engagement throughout the year. Applicants Should Carefully Consider the Weekly Commitment The Open Notebook specifically warns prospective applicants that balancing the fellowship with other commitments can be challenging. Successful fellows must be able to make sufficient time for the program and meet deadlines consistently. Among other responsibilities, participants should expect to make time for: Phone interviews with sources, which ordinarily take place during U.S. daytime hours; Weekly telephone or video meetings with their mentors; Multiple rounds of editing and revision for most articles; Story annotation as part of fact-checking; and Participation in conversations and activities within the fellowship Slack community. This consideration may be particularly important for applicants combining the fellowship with full-time employment, graduate studies, dissertations, freelance work, family responsibilities, or other substantial professional obligations. Eligibility Requirements for The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship The fellowship is intended for early-career science journalists . One of its most significant features is its international accessibility. Applicants do not have to live in the United States . The Open Notebook explicitly states that people living outside the U.S. are welcome to apply. This makes the program relevant to emerging science journalists around the world. Some Public-Facing Writing Experience Is Required Applicants must have some training and/or experience in writing for the general public. Extensive professional experience is not required. In fact, the program is specifically designed for journalists who are still relatively early in their careers. However, applicants cannot be completely without relevant experience or training. They need to demonstrate at least some background in public-facing writing. Professional Science-Writing Experience Limit Science journalists and aspiring science journalists should generally have fewer than three years of regular professional science-writing experience . There are important qualifications to this rule. Internships and student work do not count toward the fewer-than-three-years requirement. The Open Notebook may also make exceptions where an applicant has more than three years of professional science-writing experience but some or all of that professional experience was not in English . This provision can make the program more accessible to journalists who developed professionally in another language before moving into English-language science journalism. English-Language Requirements Applications must be submitted in English. This requirement extends to: Application responses; Writing samples; and Letters of recommendation. However, materials that were originally produced in another language may be translated into English and submitted. The selection criteria also indicate that applicants whose first language is not English are not expected to demonstrate flawless English writing. Nevertheless, participants need a sufficiently high level of English proficiency to work effectively within the fellowship s reporting, writing, editing, mentoring, and publication process. What The Open Notebook Looks for When Selecting Fellows Meeting the basic eligibility requirements does not automatically make an applicant competitive. The Open Notebook identifies several qualities that receive priority during selection. 1. Serious Interest in Professional Science Journalism Applicants should demonstrate a strong intention to work primarily as professional science journalists . This distinction is important. The fellowship is specifically focused on journalism rather than the much broader field of science communication. Applicants should therefore be able to demonstrate that journalism itself is central to their professional goals. 2. Experience Writing About Science for the Public Candidates should have at least some training or experience communicating science through writing intended for a general audience. The experience does not need to be extensive. 3. Understanding of the Science-Journalism Profession Strong candidates should demonstrate some awareness of: How science journalism works; Challenges commonly encountered by science journalists; Skills they currently possess; Areas in which they need additional development; and How the fellowship could help them grow professionally. Applicants should therefore approach the application as an opportunity to demonstrate both existing knowledge and a thoughtful understanding of their own development needs. 4. Familiarity With The Open Notebook Candidates should familiarize themselves with The Open Notebook and the kinds of stories it publishes . This becomes particularly important because applicants are required to propose potential TON stories as part of the application. A generic journalism proposal that does not fit The Open Notebook s editorial focus is unlikely to demonstrate the same preparation as a proposal clearly developed with the publication in mind. 5. Ability to Generate Strong Story Ideas Applicants should demonstrate that they can develop interesting and appropriate story ideas suitable for The Open Notebook. Story ideation is therefore an important part of the selection process. 6. Reliability and Commitment to Deadlines The program emphasizes conscientiousness and the ability to deliver high-quality work on schedule. Because fellows go through a rigorous editorial process involving reporting, writing, editing, revisions, fact-checking, and publication, reliability is an important professional requirement. 7. Strong Writing Ability Writing ability is another selection factor. Applicants whose first language is not English should note that The Open Notebook says it takes this into consideration and does not expect flawless English. However, participants need enough English proficiency to successfully complete a demanding English-language journalism fellowship. Required Application Materials The fellowship application requires several components. Prospective candidates can strengthen their preparation by understanding these requirements well before applications open. 1. Responses to Application Questions Applicants are asked to respond to questions addressing topics including: Why they are interested in the fellowship; What they hope to learn from participating; Previous training and/or experience writing science stories for the general public; Particular skills, interests, or perspectives they could bring to the fellowship; and Their broader plans during the fellowship period. The final area is particularly important because The Open Notebook wants to understand what other commitments applicants may have during the fellowship. For example, an applicant may simultaneously be: Completing a dissertation; Freelancing; Looking for full-time employment; Studying; Working elsewhere; or Managing another major professional commitment. Candidates should answer these questions carefully and accurately, particularly given the fellowship s significant time requirements. 2. Two Short Story Proposals Applicants must submit two short proposals for potential The Open Notebook features or multimedia stories . These should be ideas suitable for publication by TON. Possible formats include: Behind-the-story interviews with writers; Reported features examining an aspect of the craft of science writing; Roundtable discussions; or Other creative feature-length projects focused on the craft of science writing. Each proposal is approximately 100 words . These are brief proposals rather than complete, full-scale pitches. Because applicants are specifically evaluated partly on their familiarity with The Open Notebook and their ability to generate appropriate story ideas, prospective candidates should spend time reading TON before developing their proposals. 3. Resume or CV Applicants must provide a resume or curriculum vitae (CV) . The document should enable reviewers to understand the applicant s educational, writing, journalism, employment, training, and other relevant professional background. 4. One Letter of Reference Applicants need one reference letter . The reference may come from an appropriate person such as a: Professor; Editor; Mentor; Supervisor; or Professional colleague. Applicants should select someone capable of speaking meaningfully about their skills and personal or professional qualities as they relate to science journalism and participation in the fellowship. Candidates should also contact their prospective referee early rather than waiting until the final days of the application process. 5. Up to Two Writing or Multimedia Samples Candidates can submit up to two writing or multimedia samples intended for the general public. Scientific or academic writing is not appropriate for this requirement. For audio or multimedia work, applicants may place URLs linking to the work into a PDF and upload that document. Samples must be available in English, although translated work is accepted. Applicants should therefore select examples that demonstrate their ability to communicate effectively with general audiences rather than submitting highly technical academic publications simply because those pieces concern science. 6. Optional Background Information The application also provides candidates with an optional opportunity to share additional information about themselves. The Open Notebook states that it strongly encourages writers from all types of backgrounds to apply. Applicants who belong to groups or communities historically marginalized or underrepresented in U.S. journalism are invited to provide that information if they wish. Disclosure is entirely optional , and The Open Notebook states that information disclosed in this section is kept confidential. Application Deadline for the 2026 Fellowship For the 2026 fellowship cycle, applications had to be received by: 11:59 p.m. U.S. Central Time on October 31, 2025. The reference-letter deadline was later: November 7, 2025. Applicants were advised to notify their letter writers well ahead of the deadline so referees would have sufficient time to prepare thoughtful recommendations. These deadlines have now passed. What About the 2027 Fellowship Deadline? Prospective applicants should distinguish between the completed 2026 application cycle and the upcoming 2027 cycle. The Open Notebook states that applications for the 2026 fellowship period have closed and that it expects to open applications for the 2027 fellowship by late September 2026 . The supplied program information does not provide the 2027 application deadline . Therefore, prospective 2027 applicants should not assume that October 31 will automatically be the next deadline. They should check the official 2027 fellowship announcement once applications open for the confirmed closing date and any updated program requirements. How Prospective 2027 Applicants Can Prepare Although the next application period has not yet opened according to the supplied information, prospective candidates can use the time before the launch to prepare. Step 1: Read The Open Notebook Extensively Candidates should become familiar with TON s editorial approach and the subjects it covers. This preparation can help applicants understand what constitutes an appropriate story idea and make their two short proposals substantially more relevant. Step 2: Review Your Professional Experience Applicants should determine whether they satisfy the early-career experience requirement, particularly the guideline concerning fewer than three years of regular professional science-writing experience. Remember that internships and student work are excluded from that calculation. Step 3: Select Potential Work Samples Review previously published or completed public-facing journalism and identify up to two strong samples. Candidates whose strongest work was originally published in another language can consider preparing English translations because translated materials are permitted. Step 4: Identify a Strong Referee Consider who can provide the most meaningful assessment of your potential as a science journalist. The best referee is not necessarily the person with the most prestigious title. A professor, editor, supervisor, mentor, or colleague who knows your work well may be better positioned to provide a detailed recommendation. Step 5: Develop Potential TON Story Ideas Because two short proposals form part of the application, candidates can begin observing recurring questions, challenges, techniques, and emerging issues in the craft of science journalism. Ideas can then be evaluated against the kinds of stories The Open Notebook actually publishes. Step 6: Assess Your Availability Before applying, consider whether you can realistically commit to the fellowship for an entire year. The estimated five-to-seven-hour average weekly workload should not be interpreted as a guaranteed maximum. Reporting deadlines, revisions, interviews, and fact-checking may make particular weeks significantly busier. Why This Fellowship Can Be Valuable for Early-Career Science Journalists The structure of The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship brings together several forms of professional development that emerging journalists often need simultaneously. Fellows receive: Practical reporting assignments; Publication opportunities; One-on-one mentorship; Editorial guidance; Repeated feedback and revision experience; Exposure to professional fact-checking processes; Experience developing and pitching story ideas; Participation in an editorial community; Contact with current and former fellows; Career-development guidance; and Financial support through the fellowship stipend. The combination of mentoring and actual publication work is particularly significant. Fellows are not simply learning about journalism in theory; they are expected to practice the reporting, writing, revision, and deadline-management processes required in professional journalism. Important Considerations Before Applying Prospective applicants should carefully consider several questions before submitting an application: Do I genuinely intend to pursue journalism? The program prioritizes applicants who want professional science journalism, rather than other forms of science communication, to be their primary professional direction. Do I have enough relevant experience to qualify? Applicants need some training or experience writing for the general public, even though extensive experience is not required. Am I still within the early-career experience range? Applicants should review the fewer-than-three-years professional science-writing guideline and its stated exceptions. Can I work effectively in English? Perfect English is not expected from applicants who speak it as an additional language, but sufficient proficiency is necessary to participate successfully. Can I make time for the program? Five to seven hours per week is an average estimate, and some periods can demand considerably more time. Can I reliably meet deadlines? Fellows need to complete stories, revisions, fact-checking preparations, meetings, and other responsibilities according to schedule. Do I understand The Open Notebook? Familiarity with the publication is an explicit selection consideration and is particularly important when developing the two proposed story ideas. APPLY NOW Conclusion The The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program offers emerging science journalists an opportunity to develop professional skills through a combination of mentorship, reporting, writing, editing, publication, and community participation. The remote, part-time structure makes the fellowship accessible to applicants beyond the United States, while its focus on early-career journalists provides developing writers with an opportunity to learn directly from experienced science-journalism professionals. For the 2026 fellowship period, the program offered a $6,600 stipend , lasted 12 months , began on February 23, 2026 , and required an estimated average commitment of approximately five to seven hours per week . The 2026 application deadline was October 31, 2025, at 11:59 p.m. U.S. Central Time , with reference letters due November 7, 2025. That application cycle is now closed. The next important date for prospective applicants is therefore the expected opening of the 2027 fellowship application cycle by late September 2026 . Since the supplied information does not specify the 2027 deadline, prospective applicants should monitor The Open Notebook s official fellowship information for the new application announcement and confirmed deadline. In the meantime, potential candidates can prepare by reading The Open Notebook s journalism, developing appropriate story ideas, identifying strong work samples and a suitable referee, reviewing their eligibility, and ensuring they can make the substantial year-long commitment the fellowship requires. For aspiring and early-career science journalists seeking structured mentorship, professional editorial experience, published work, and deeper involvement in the international science-journalism community, The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship is an opportunity worth preparing for well before the next application window opens. If you have any questions, please email TON executive director and editor-in-chief Siri Carpenter: siricarpenter@theopennotebook.com . Visit the OFY website for more Fellowship Opportunities . title: Scottish Government Policy & Events Traineeship 2026 in Brussels: Apply for the 12-Month Paid Programme
summary: Applications are now open for the Scottish Government Policy Events Traineeship 2026 , an exciting 12-month professional opportunity based at Scotland House Brussels in Belgium . The programme provides an opportunity to gain practical professional experience at the centre of European policymaking while contributing to Scotland s engagement with European Union institutions, member states and other European organisations. The British Diplomatic Missions in Brussels are recruiting for the Policy Events Traineeship for the Scottish Government EU Office at Scotland House Brussels . The successful trainee will gain experience across policy research, European affairs, stakeholder engagement, event management, ministerial visits, communications and wider team activities. The traineeship is a full-time, 12-month placement , with the successful candidate expected to begin on 2 November 2026 . The position carries a professional immersion indemnity of €1,500 per month , alongside additional benefits. Interested candidates should pay particularly close attention to the eligibility conditions. Most importantly, candidates must already possess the independent right to live and work in Belgium and must be able to maintain that right throughout the traineeship. The application deadline is 19 August 2026 at 23:55, Belgium local time . Candidates are strongly encouraged not to wait until the final minutes to submit their applications. About the Scottish Government Policy Events Traineeship 2026 The Policy Events Traineeship provides a 12-month opportunity to develop professional skills and experience across a variety of areas while working in Brussels. The trainee will support the Scottish Government s four core policy priorities for 2026–2027, particularly work relating to sustainability and economic growth . The role will also contribute to efforts aimed at growing Scotland s economy through innovation, investment and business support. A significant advantage of this traineeship is the breadth of exposure available to the successful candidate. Rather than concentrating exclusively on one narrow area of work, the trainee will have opportunities to participate in policy monitoring, research, written reporting, event organisation, stakeholder engagement and official visits. The trainee will work closely with the EU Engagement and Bilateral Relations Lead and the Events and Visits Manager . This includes helping to organise the office s core annual programme of events and supporting additional activities hosted at the Scotland House Conference Centre and external venues. Events may take place both online and in person . The successful candidate will also help coordinate visits to Brussels by Ministers and senior stakeholders, in addition to supporting the management and welcoming of regular visitors to Scotland House. About Scotland House Brussels Scotland House Brussels operates in the heart of the EU district in Brussels and has worked for more than 20 years to promote Scottish interests and engage with EU institutions, member states and other European organisations. Its strategic location enables Scotland to maintain relationships with European institutions and partners and provides a platform through which Scottish interests, expertise and achievements can be promoted. The Scottish Government EU Office works across numerous policy areas. These include research and innovation, renewable energy, equalities and other important areas. Scotland House also hosts events designed to showcase Scotland s cultural reputation, including its food, drink and hospitality. Another organisation based at Scotland House is Scottish Development International (SDI) , Scotland s trade and inward investment agency. SDI works with businesses and investors interested in trading with, establishing operations in or investing in Scotland. It provides information, connections, advice and other forms of support and operates through a global network of more than 30 offices. Working in this environment therefore offers the trainee exposure to the intersection of public policy, European affairs, international relations, economic development, investment, cultural diplomacy and stakeholder engagement. What Will the Policy Events Trainee Do? The successful applicant will undertake responsibilities covering several major areas. 1. Support Policy Teams Across Different Policy Areas Policy monitoring and analysis form an important part of the traineeship. The trainee will help monitor EU policy developments and gain insights into emerging issues by using open-source information and engaging with relevant stakeholders. Responsibilities may include: Monitoring developments in EU and European policy; Researching relevant policy issues through open-source information; Engaging with key stakeholders to develop policy insights; Supporting updates for Scottish Government policy colleagues; Contributing to information provided to Scottish Ministers; Helping prepare weekly notes distributed across different Scottish Government departments; Promoting Scotland s achievements; and Identifying and encouraging opportunities for collaboration in addressing shared challenges. For candidates hoping to develop careers involving public policy, European affairs, government, international relations, research or public administration, these responsibilities provide practical exposure to how information is gathered, analysed and communicated within a governmental environment. 2. Support Cultural Diplomacy and Policy Events Events are another major component of the traineeship. The successful candidate will work alongside the Events Team to support both cultural diplomacy events and policy-themed events . Activities can include: Drafting event notes; Preparing event-related materials; Producing communication materials; Issuing invitations; Monitoring invitations and responses; Ordering catering; Arranging supplies; Supporting event logistics; Helping deliver events at Scotland House and external venues; Supporting both online and in-person activities; and Assisting with the organisation of visits by Ministers and senior stakeholders. This part of the programme provides practical experience in professional event coordination while allowing the trainee to understand how events can support policy engagement, relationship-building and cultural diplomacy. 3. Support Ministerial and Senior Stakeholder Visits The trainee will assist in organising visits to Brussels by Ministers and senior stakeholders. This can include supporting engagement with: EU institutions; Brussels-based networks; Partner organisations; and Other relevant stakeholders. The trainee will therefore gain insight into the planning and coordination required to support high-level governmental and stakeholder engagements. 4. Welcome and Coordinate Visitors to Scotland House Brussels Scotland House regularly receives visitors, and the trainee will contribute to ensuring that visitors have a smooth and professional experience. The role includes supporting the coordination and welcoming of visitors and helping manage regular visits to Scotland House. This aspect of the position requires strong organisational, communication and interpersonal skills. 5. Attend External Meetings The successful trainee may attend external meetings both online and in person. Following these engagements, the trainee may be responsible for providing reports and updates to colleagues. This offers an opportunity to strengthen listening, analytical, note-taking, reporting and professional communication skills. 6. Contribute to Wider Mission Activities The traineeship extends beyond the trainee s immediate policy and events responsibilities. The successful candidate may participate in wider Mission initiatives and take on a corporate role where required. This provides broader exposure to the operations and priorities of the organisation. Learning and Professional Development Opportunities Professional development is an important component of the programme. The Scottish Government provides employees with access to a broad range of training opportunities. Depending on the trainee s responsibilities and interests, they may be able to choose from a comprehensive training catalogue to develop relevant professional capabilities. The traineeship also provides some flexibility according to the successful candidate s abilities, interests and career aspirations. As the placement progresses, the team may review the trainee s responsibilities and help them develop further in areas they are particularly interested in. This flexibility means that the programme can provide more than routine work experience. The trainee may have opportunities to gradually develop responsibilities and capabilities that contribute to longer-term career development. Essential Qualifications, Skills and Experience Candidates should carefully review the essential requirements before submitting an application. The ideal candidate must demonstrate the following: Fluent English: Applicants need written and spoken English at CEFR C1 level or higher . Higher education: Candidates must possess a relevant higher education degree. Relevant experience: Applicants should have relevant academic, employment or voluntary experience. Interest in European policy: Candidates should demonstrate a keen interest in EU and European policy. Knowledge of the EU: Applicants should understand EU institutions and processes. Research ability: Strong research skills are required. Writing ability: Candidates need good professional writing skills. Time and workload management: Applicants should be capable of prioritising their workload and delivering work within tight deadlines. Communication: Strong communication skills are essential. Interpersonal skills: Candidates should be able to interact effectively with colleagues and stakeholders. Teamwork: The role requires strong team-working capabilities. IT proficiency: Applicants need strong IT skills, including experience using Microsoft Office. Applicants invited to interview should also be aware that their language skills may be assessed during the recruitment process. Desirable Skills and Experience In addition to the essential criteria, certain qualifications and experiences would strengthen an application. These include: Familiarity with Scotland; Knowledge of Scottish politics and culture; A passion for promoting Scotland; French language skills; Dutch language skills; Skills in other languages; and Previous experience supporting or organising events. These are described as desirable rather than essential criteria. Key Behaviours Expected from Applicants Candidates are expected to demonstrate several important professional behaviours throughout the selection process and traineeship. These include: Communicating and Influencing Delivering at Pace Managing a Quality Service Working Together Prospective applicants should therefore consider examples from their academic studies, employment, volunteering or other relevant experiences that demonstrate these behaviours. Duration and Working Arrangements This is a full-time professional immersion traineeship lasting 12 months . The working schedule consists of: 36.25 net working hours per week Five working days per week 12-month traineeship duration Location: Brussels, Belgium Expected start date: 2 November 2026 Number of available positions: One Candidates should consider the full 12-month commitment before applying. Salary and Financial Benefits The professional immersion indemnity attached to the position is €1,500 per month . Additional benefits include: Commute/public transport reimbursement; and Luncheon vouchers worth €8 per working day . The vacancy also specifies different tax arrangements for Belgian and non-Belgian nationals. Belgian nationals will receive their salary gross and are expected to fulfil their tax obligations by completing the relevant tax return with Belgian authorities. Non-Belgian nationals will receive their salary net after the deduction of an amount equivalent to Belgian tax retained at source. Candidates progressing through the recruitment process will receive further information about these arrangements. Annual Leave During the Traineeship Trainees have access to: One day of paid annual leave per month of the traineeship; and One day of unpaid leave per month of the traineeship. Applicants should take these conditions into account when assessing the overall terms of the programme. Important Requirement Regarding University or School Programmes Candidates should pay particular attention to the nature of this placement. This is a professional immersion traineeship outside any educational programme . As a result, the organisation states that paperwork with a university or school cannot be signed for the traineeship. Students or recent graduates who require an internship agreement, university placement agreement or similar documentation from the host organisation should therefore carefully consider this condition before applying. Age and Medical Coverage Requirements Applicants must meet the professional immersion traineeship requirements. Candidates must: Be at least 18 years old ; and Provide proof of valid medical coverage for the entire traineeship period, such as a European or Global Health Insurance Card . The successful candidate will also be subject to professional background checks and security clearance. Right to Live and Work in Belgium One of the most important eligibility conditions concerns immigration and employment status. Candidates must currently hold an independent right to live and work in Belgium . They must also be prepared to ensure that this legal right remains valid throughout the duration of the contract. The responsibility for satisfying Belgium s legal requirements for living and working in the country rests with the applicant. Prospective international applicants should therefore verify that they independently meet this condition before spending significant time preparing an application. Travel, Interview and Relocation Expenses Applicants should also budget appropriately if participation requires travel or relocation. The British Diplomatic Missions will not cover travel expenses incurred when travelling to an interview . Similarly, relocation expenses will not be covered if a candidate is offered the traineeship. Candidates who do not already live in Brussels should therefore consider potential accommodation, relocation and associated living costs when determining whether the opportunity is financially suitable for them. Employment Conditions Locally recruited staff working for the British Diplomatic Missions in Belgium are subject to Terms and Conditions of Service in accordance with local Belgian employment law . The successful candidate will also have to complete the required professional background checks and security clearance before taking up the position. How to Apply for the Policy Events Traineeship 2026 Candidates should submit their application through the official British Government recruitment platform operated through tal.net/Oleeo . Applicants are advised to: Carefully review all eligibility and professional immersion requirements. Confirm that they already possess an independent right to live and work in Belgium. Ensure their English proficiency meets the required CEFR C1 level or above. Review their academic, work and voluntary experience against the essential criteria. Prepare examples demonstrating the required professional behaviours. Complete all required sections of the online application. Review the application carefully for errors or missing information. Submit the completed application before the deadline. The vacancy specifically warns applicants that applications for Country Based Staff positions with the British Government can only be submitted through the official tal.net recruitment website operated by Oleeo . Although vacancies may also appear on third-party websites, those advertisements should ultimately direct applicants to the official recruitment platform. Applications submitted through another website will not be received by the British Government recruitment system. APPLY NOW Policy Events Traineeship 2026 Application Deadline The application deadline is 19 August 2026 . Applications must be submitted by 23:55 on 19 August 2026 , according to the local time zone of the country where the vacancy is located. Since this position is based in Brussels, applicants should work according to the applicable Belgium local time . Candidates should avoid waiting until the final hour to complete their applications. Only applications that have been fully completed and submitted before the deadline will be considered. Key Dates Application deadline: 19 August 2026 Closing time: 23:55, Belgium local time Expected start date: 2 November 2026 Programme duration: 12 months Why Consider the Scottish Government Policy Events Traineeship? The programme provides a distinctive combination of policy and practical professional experience. A successful trainee could gain exposure to: EU and European policy developments; Scottish Government policy priorities; Government research and reporting; Ministerial engagement; International stakeholder relations; Cultural diplomacy; Event planning and management; Communications; European institutions and Brussels-based networks; Economic growth, innovation and investment policy; Professional writing; Official visits and stakeholder coordination; and Working within an international governmental environment. The position could be particularly valuable for someone seeking to build experience relevant to future careers in policy, European affairs, public administration, international relations, government, stakeholder engagement, communications or professional event management. Equality, Diversity and Inclusion The British Government describes itself as an inclusive and diversity-friendly employer. It states that it values difference, promotes equality and challenges discrimination while encouraging applications from people of all backgrounds. The employer states that it does not discriminate based on disability, race, colour, ethnicity, gender identity, religion, sexual orientation, age, veteran status or other categories protected by law. The organisation also promotes family-friendly flexible working opportunities where operational and security requirements permit. Final Application Checklist Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should confirm that they: Are at least 18 years old; Hold a relevant higher education degree; Have relevant academic, professional or voluntary experience; Have English proficiency at CEFR C1 level or higher; Have a strong interest in EU or European policy; Understand EU institutions and processes; Possess strong research and writing skills; Can work effectively under tight deadlines; Have strong communication, interpersonal and teamwork skills; Have good IT skills, including Microsoft Office; Already possess an independent right to live and work in Belgium; Can maintain that right throughout the traineeship; Can provide valid medical coverage for the traineeship period; Understand that university or school paperwork cannot be signed for this placement; Understand that interview travel and relocation expenses will not be covered; and Can submit a complete application by 23:55 Belgium local time on 19 August 2026 . title: Constellations Fellowship Fall 2026: Apply for 55 Remote Climate Roles With a $1,000 Completion Stipend
summary: Applications are now open for the Constellations Fellowship Fall 2026, an international professional-development programme connecting students and recent graduates with climate-focused organisations around the world. The Fall 2026 cycle offers 55 virtual, part-time placements covering climate justice, sustainability, carbon analysis, environmental research, finance, business development, communications, monitoring and evaluation, data science, engineering, agriculture, waste management, circular economy and other areas. The programme will run for approximately 12 to 14 weeks, beginning on Monday, September 21, 2026. Each selected fellow will work remotely with a participating host organisation and will receive a $1,000 stipend after completing the fellowship. Applications are open to students and recent graduates worldwide, except candidates located in countries affected by applicable international sanctions. The application deadline is Sunday, August 23, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EST, as stated in the official Fall 2026 application form . What Is the Constellations Fellowship? The Constellations Fellowship is a professional virtual internship programme operated by Climate Curve. It connects students and recent graduates with career opportunities in Climate Curve’s global network of climate organisations, including organisations associated with the Keeling Curve Prize. According to the official Constellations Fellowship page , the programme is designed to foster the next generation of climate leaders by giving early-career participants practical, entry-level experience. Rather than following a single academic curriculum, fellows work directly with host organisations on defined professional assignments. Depending on the selected position, a fellow may contribute to research, data analysis, communications, engineering, programme management, environmental justice, finance, marketing, partnerships or operational work. The experience is intended to help participants develop: Practical workplace experience; Career-building skills; Professional confidence; Remote collaboration skills; Knowledge of climate organisations and climate solutions; Experience completing real assignments; Exposure to multidisciplinary climate work; and A stronger understanding of how climate organisations operate. About Climate Curve Climate Curve is a United States-based nonprofit organisation formerly known as the Global Warming Mitigation Project. Its mission is to contribute to global decarbonisation by identifying climate leaders and deploying resources to advance effective solutions. The organisation works to accelerate projects and programmes that reduce, remove or replace greenhouse-gas emissions. Its broader approach includes providing capital, professional talent and visibility to climate initiatives. Climate Curve recognises that climate innovation is increasing, but the funding and workforce talent needed to scale effective solutions remain inadequate. It therefore connects entrepreneurs, organisations, funders, researchers, professionals and emerging climate leaders through different programmes. The Constellations Fellowship addresses the workforce component of this challenge by connecting emerging professionals with climate organisations that need additional skills and capacity. More information about the organisation’s mission and approach is available on the Climate Curve About page . Fellowship Duration and Working Arrangement The Fall 2026 fellowships are entirely virtual and part-time. All placements are expected to begin on Monday, September 21, 2026, and continue for approximately 12 to 14 weeks. The precise schedule and weekly workload may differ by host organisation and position. Candidates should carefully review the individual description of their selected role because some host organisations specify particular weekly time commitments, technical expectations, meeting requirements or time-zone preferences. The general programme information does not establish one standard number of weekly working hours for every position. Applicants should therefore confirm that they can meet the requirements of the particular role before applying. Because the fellowships are fully remote, successful candidates will normally need: Reliable internet access; A suitable computer; Availability for online meetings; The ability to work independently; Effective written and verbal communication; Time-management skills; and The ability to collaborate across locations and time zones. These are practical expectations for remote participation. Candidates must still consult the official position page for the actual desired qualifications of each placement. Constellations Fellowship Stipend Fellows will receive a $1,000 stipend upon completion of the fellowship. Applicants should understand the payment arrangement correctly: The amount is a total fellowship stipend, not a monthly payment; It is not described as an hourly wage; It is not stated to be paid at the beginning of the programme; Payment is linked to completion of the fellowship; and The application form does not explain payment methods, tax treatment or the precise completion requirements. Candidates requiring clarification regarding stipend payment should contact the programme manager before accepting a placement. Benefits of the Constellations Fellowship 1. Fully remote participation Candidates can participate from their home countries without relocating to the host organisation’s office. 2. Practical climate-sector experience Fellows work with organisations addressing real climate, environmental and sustainability challenges rather than completing only theoretical coursework. 3. Entry-level career exposure The programme is designed for students and recent graduates who may not yet have extensive professional experience. 4. Diverse professional pathways Applicants are not limited to environmental science positions. The Fall 2026 opportunities include finance, accounting, marketing, communications, design, engineering, data science, monitoring and evaluation, research, partnerships, sales, operations and software development. 5. International organisational exposure Participants can gain experience working with organisations operating across different regions and climate sectors. 6. Career-building skills The programme aims to help fellows develop practical workplace, project-management, communication, research, technical and professional skills. 7. Step 5: Follow the programme’s artificial-intelligence rule The application form expressly states that applicants must submit a cover letter written in their own voice. The use of artificial-intelligence tools to generate or substantially refine the cover letter is prohibited and may result in disqualification. Candidates should therefore write and edit their application materials themselves. They should not use AI to draft, rewrite or significantly polish their cover letters. Step 6: Enter contact information The form requires the applicant’s: First name; Last name; and Email address. Candidates should use an active email account that they regularly monitor. Step 7: Submit a complete application Incomplete applications will not be accepted. The form warns that incomplete or low-quality materials will not be considered. Uploading the same résumé in both document fields will also make the application invalid. Before submission, verify that: The correct position has been selected; The résumé is complete and no longer than one page; The résumé is in PDF format; The cover letter is complete and in PDF format; The cover letter is addressed to the host organisation; The documents are tailored to the selected position; The correct documents have been uploaded in the correct fields; and The application has been submitted before the deadline. A separate application must be completed for every position. Each submission must include the appropriate résumé and cover letter for that particular host organisation and role. Reusing generic application materials without tailoring them to the separate positions may be treated as a low-quality application. Applicants should not upload a transcript, résumé or recommendation letter in the cover-letter field. Application Deadline Applications close on: Sunday, August 23, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EST. Candidates should submit early because: Incomplete applications are rejected; Separate applications are required for multiple positions; Both documents must be converted to PDF; Technical problems can occur during uploading; The published time-zone label may differ from an applicant’s local time; and Late submissions may not be accepted. Important Information Not Specified in the General Form The general application does not state: The number of fellows who will ultimately be selected; Whether every listed position will accept only one fellow; A single weekly-hour requirement applicable to all positions; The method or timing of stipend payment beyond payment upon completion; The tax treatment of the stipend; Whether a completion certificate will be issued; Whether fellows receive future employment consideration; The exact definition of a recent graduate; A universal academic-discipline requirement; or A definitive list of countries affected by the sanctions restriction. Candidates requiring answers to these questions should contact the programme directly rather than make assumptions. Practical Application Tips Match the position carefully Apply where your background genuinely meets the role’s responsibilities and desired qualifications. A precise application is stronger than applying indiscriminately to many positions. Keep the résumé disciplined The one-page limit is mandatory. Prioritise the education, skills, projects and experience most relevant to the selected position. Research the host organisation Your cover letter should demonstrate that you understand the host organisation’s work and the contribution expected from the fellow. Use your authentic voice The programme specifically prohibits AI-generated or substantially AI-edited cover letters. Write naturally and explain your motivation through your own experiences. Check availability before applying Confirm that you can begin on September 21, 2026, remain available for 12 to 14 weeks and meet the weekly commitment specified by the host organisation. Create a new application for every role Do not assume that selecting multiple positions or submitting a generic application will be accepted. Each position requires a complete, separate submission. Review every upload Make sure the résumé is in the résumé field and the cover letter is in the cover-letter field. Uploading the résumé twice will result in an incomplete application. Contact Information Questions may be directed to Saige Middleton, Programme Manager, at: s.middleton@climatecurve.org Applicants should ask questions early enough to allow time for a response before the deadline. Conclusion The Constellations Fellowship Fall 2026 offers students and recent graduates an opportunity to gain practical experience with climate organisations while working remotely from eligible locations worldwide. With 55 positions across climate justice, sustainability, finance, engineering, communications, carbon analysis, circular economy, agriculture, waste management, monitoring and evaluation, the programme accommodates a wide range of academic and professional interests. Candidates applying for more than one position must submit a separate application for each role. Complete applications must be submitted by Sunday, August 23, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EST. title: Digital Wellness Lab Student Advisory Council 2026–2027: U.S. Teens Can Work with Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School on Digital Wellness and AI
summary: Applications are now open for the Digital Wellness Lab Student Advisory Council 2026–2027 , a virtual youth leadership initiative that gives teenagers and young adults across the United States an opportunity to influence research, technology design, digital wellness initiatives, and discussions about the future of artificial intelligence. Now entering its fifth year , the Student Advisory Council is the flagship youth initiative of the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School . A small group of selected students works directly with researchers, clinicians, technology-industry leaders, policy influencers, and other experts throughout the academic year. For the 2026–2027 cycle, the Council introduces two participation tracks: Changemakers and Architects . The tracks recognize that young people face two interconnected challenges: learning how to live healthily with the technology that already surrounds them and helping shape the emerging technologies that will define the future. The programme runs from October 2026 through May 2027 , with all regular Council meetings taking place virtually. Applications close on 7 September 2026 at 11:59 PM Eastern Time . About the Digital Wellness Lab Student Advisory Council The Digital Wellness Lab Student Advisory Council gives young people a meaningful role in conversations about technology, online life, digital wellbeing, artificial intelligence, social media, gaming, mental health, and emerging digital environments. Rather than treating teenagers simply as research subjects or technology users, the programme invites them to become active contributors. Council members share their experiences of growing up in a highly connected world and help researchers and decision-makers understand how technology actually affects young people s daily lives. Participants may contribute to: Digital wellness research Youth-focused resources Technology recommendations Discussions with technology companies AI and emerging-technology testing Community projects Research studies Teen Voices publications Policy and industry conversations Their perspectives may help shape what the Digital Wellness Lab studies next and how researchers, clinicians, technology creators, and policymakers approach online environments used by young people. Who Organizes the Programme? The Student Advisory Council is organized by the Digital Wellness Lab , which works in connection with Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School. Council members may engage with: Researchers Clinicians Digital wellness specialists Technology-industry professionals AI developers Trust and safety leaders Policy influencers Youth advocates The programme therefore combines youth participation with exposure to research, healthcare, technology, and public-policy perspectives. Programme Duration The 2026–2027 Student Advisory Council runs from: October 2026 to May 2027 The programme begins with a virtual kickoff in early October and continues throughout the academic year. Participants will engage in projects, sessions, research activities, industry conversations, and collaborative learning before presenting their work in spring 2027. New for 2026–2027: Two Participation Tracks For the first time, applicants can choose between two different pathways: Changemakers Architects Applicants complete a single application and rank their preferred track. Although the two pathways have different age ranges, time commitments, and project outcomes, students in both tracks can contribute directly to Digital Wellness Lab research and may publish content through the Lab’s Teen Voices platform. Track A: Changemakers Put Digital Wellness Research into Action The Changemakers track is designed for students who want to address digital challenges that already affect their schools, communities, friends, and peers. Participants may explore issues such as: Social media Smartphone use School phone policies Gaming Online mental health Digital wellbeing Online relationships Screen time Healthy technology habits Each Changemaker will identify a particular digital wellness challenge affecting their school or community. They will then explore relevant research, identify possible responses, and develop an individual project with support from a Digital Wellness Lab mentor. Who Can Join the Changemakers Track? Changemakers should be: 14–18 years old U.S. high school students In grades 9–12 Age eligibility is calculated based on the applicant’s age on 1 October 2026 . Time Commitment Participants should expect approximately: 3–4 hours per month The programme is virtual. What Changemakers Will Produce Each participant will develop: An individual action project addressing a digital wellness issue in their school or community. The track is particularly suited to students who already see a technology-related challenge around them and want to move from observation to practical action. Track B: Architects Help Shape the Future of Technology The Architects track focuses more heavily on emerging technologies and the digital environments young people will use in the future. Participants will engage with topics including: Artificial intelligence Generative AI Chatbots Emerging digital platforms Technology design Youth online safety Responsible innovation Healthy digital environments Architects will work as a group to share their perspectives with people involved in developing and influencing new technologies. Who Can Join the Architects Track? Architects should be: 16–20 years old U.S. students From approximately 11th grade through the second year of college Past Student Advisory Council members are also invited to apply. Age eligibility is based on the applicant’s age on 1 October 2026 . Time Commitment Architects should expect a larger commitment of approximately: 8–10 hours per month Activities remain virtual. What Architects Will Produce Architects may contribute to: Co-authored industry recommendations Published recommendations for technology companies Hands-on testing of emerging AI tools Feedback on future digital environments Research and youth-perspective publications This track is best suited to young people who are interested in how AI and emerging technology should be designed safely and responsibly. What Council Members Will Experience Regardless of which track they join, participants will gain exposure to several dimensions of digital wellness research and leadership. Work with Experts Council members will have opportunities to learn from and interact with researchers and clinicians connected to Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School . Participants can gain insight into how researchers study young people’s relationships with technology and translate findings into practical recommendations. Engage with Technology Decision-Makers Students may share their perspectives directly with people working in the technology sector, including individuals involved in: AI development Product design Trust and safety Online wellbeing Digital policy Young people therefore gain an unusual opportunity to communicate directly with adults whose decisions may influence the platforms and technologies they use. Contribute to Research Both Changemakers and Architects may contribute to Digital Wellness Lab research studies. Young people can help researchers understand technology not simply through statistics but through lived experience. Publish Through Teen Voices Council members may also have opportunities to publish their perspectives through the Digital Wellness Lab’s Teen Voices platform. Teen Voices features youth perspectives on issues related to growing up online. Previous topics have included: Screen time Digital relationships and trust School phone restrictions Youth safety online Algorithmic influence Why Youth Perspectives Matter Young people are among the most active users of digital technology, yet decisions about technology are often made without sustained youth participation. The Student Advisory Council seeks to change that by bringing young people directly into research and design conversations. Council members can explain how digital environments affect: Friendships School experiences Mental health Identity Family relationships Communication Community participation Creativity Learning Personal safety These perspectives can help researchers and technology leaders understand problems that may not be visible through adult observation alone. Application Process The application is designed to be relatively accessible. Applicants should expect the form to take approximately: 20–30 minutes The application includes short-answer questions. No individual response should exceed: 250 words Students should therefore aim to communicate clearly and specifically rather than writing long essays. Finalist Interviews Students selected as finalists will be invited to participate in a brief video interview before the final selection decision. Applicants should be prepared to discuss: Why they care about digital wellness Their experiences with technology Which track interests them What issues they want to explore What they hope to contribute How they might use the experience in their school or community Important Dates Applicants should keep the following timeline in mind: 10 August 2026: Applications open 7 September 2026: Applications close 7 September 2026 at 11:59 PM ET: Final application deadline 18 September 2026: Council member announcement listed in the programme timeline Early October 2026: Virtual kickoff October 2026–May 2027: Projects, sessions, research participation, and industry conversations Spring 2027: Final presentations The application materials also state that selected finalists will be notified in late September and invited to a short video interview. Because this timing differs slightly from the programme timeline listing 18 September for Council member announcements, applicants should follow the latest information provided through the official application portal. Is the Programme Virtual? Yes. The regular Student Advisory Council activities are conducted virtually. This allows selected students from different parts of the United States to participate without relocating or regularly travelling to Boston. Applicants should nevertheless ensure that they can commit to the time expectations associated with their selected track. Time Commitment The expected monthly commitment depends on the track. Changemakers Approximately: 3–4 hours per month Architects Approximately: 8–10 hours per month Students should consider schoolwork, extracurricular activities, employment, family responsibilities, and other commitments before choosing their preferred track. Which Track Should You Choose? Applicants interested in solving problems affecting young people today may find Changemakers the stronger fit. Consider Changemakers if you want to: Improve digital wellbeing in your school Address smartphone use Explore healthier social-media habits Develop a community project Turn research into action Applicants interested in technology development and the future of AI may prefer Architects. Consider Architects if you want to: Discuss responsible AI Test emerging AI tools Influence technology designers Develop recommendations for industry Explore how future digital environments should be built Applicants submit one application and can rank their preferred track. Eligibility Requirements Eligibility differs between the two tracks. Changemakers Eligibility Applicants should: Be aged 14–18 as of 1 October 2026 Be a U.S. high school student Be enrolled in grades 9–12 Be interested in digital wellness and youth technology issues Be able to participate virtually Be able to commit approximately 3–4 hours per month Architects Eligibility Applicants should: Be aged 16–20 as of 1 October 2026 Be a U.S. high school or college student Generally be between 11th grade and college sophomore level Be interested in AI, digital environments, or emerging technology Be able to participate virtually Commit approximately 8–10 hours per month Past Council members are welcome to apply for the Architects track. Application Deadline The deadline for the Digital Wellness Lab Student Advisory Council 2026–2027 is: 7 September 2026 at 11:59 PM Eastern Time Applications submitted after the deadline may not be considered. Students are encouraged not to wait until the final day, particularly because the application requires thoughtful short responses. How to Apply Interested students can review the programme details and access the application through the official Digital Wellness Lab website: APPLY HERE The application takes approximately 20–30 minutes to complete. Applicants should read the track descriptions carefully before ranking their preference. Questions and Support Students, parents, teachers, counselors, and youth-organization leaders who have questions may contact the Digital Wellness Lab. Email: dwl@childrens.harvard.edu The Lab welcomes questions from both young applicants and adults helping students understand the programme. Information for Teachers, Counselors and Youth Organizations Educators and youth advocates are encouraged to share the opportunity with students who: Have strong opinions about technology Are interested in digital wellbeing Care about online safety Want to explore AI Demonstrate leadership potential Are interested in research Want their perspectives heard Care about improving their school or community The programme may be particularly valuable for students whose lived experiences can bring perspectives that technology developers and researchers might otherwise overlook. Conclusion The Digital Wellness Lab Student Advisory Council 2026–2027 gives young people in the United States an unusual opportunity to move from being everyday technology users to active contributors in conversations about digital wellbeing, AI, online safety, research, and technology design. Through its two new tracks, the programme accommodates different kinds of youth leadership. Changemakers , aged 14–18, will turn digital wellness research into practical community action through individual projects. Architects , aged 16–20, will focus on AI and emerging technology, helping develop recommendations for healthier digital environments. Participants will work virtually with experts connected to Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School while engaging with researchers, technology leaders, and policy influencers. Applications opened on 10 August 2026 and close on 7 September 2026 at 11:59 PM ET . For teenagers and young adults who have something meaningful to say about the technologies shaping their lives, this programme provides a rare opportunity to make sure those ideas reach people who can act on them. title: Numun Fund SGS 3.0 Applications 2026: Up to USD 100,000 for Feminist Tech Organising in the Larger Majority World
