Numun Fund SGS 3.0: Key Information at a Glance Programme detail Information Programme name Seed, Grow and Sustain 3.0 Common abbreviation SGS 3.0 Organising institution Numun Fund Total allocation USD 1.75 million Funding available per selected applicant USD 10,000 to USD 100,000 Funding period Two years Funding levels Seed, Grow and Sustain Primary focus Feminist technology activism and movement organising Eligible applicant types Initiatives, collectives, groups and organisations Minimum group size At least two people Registration requirement Registered, unregistered, formally organised and online-only initiatives may apply Application language English Application method Online eligibility check followed by a full application Application deadline Sunday, 6 September 2026 at 23:59 Anywhere on Earth Expected status notification January 2027 Official information Numun Fund SGS 3.0 For applicants in Pakistan, the official deadline corresponds to Monday, 7 September 2026 at 4:59 p.m. Pakistan Standard Time. Applicants are nevertheless strongly advised to submit well before the final hours because the official closing time is expressed in the Anywhere on Earth time zone. About Numun Fund Numun Fund describes itself as a feminist technology fund grounded in and led by the movements it seeks to serve. Its central objective is to seed, resource and sustain an ecosystem of feminist activists who can define, imagine, shape and challenge technology according to the realities and priorities of their communities. The word “Numun” means “seed” in Sumerian. The name reflects the fund’s recognition that art, science and technology have historically been shaped by communities in what Numun calls the Larger Majority World. The fund was created as a response to two closely connected challenges: Technology has become increasingly important to movement organising, political participation, community safety, economic inclusion and social justice. Funding and decision-making power surrounding technology remain heavily concentrated in the Global North, while communities most affected by technological systems are frequently excluded from determining how those systems are designed and governed. Numun Fund therefore seeks to move resources and decision-making power towards feminist activists and movements in historically under-resourced regions and communities. What Is the Seed, Grow and Sustain 3.0 Programme? Seed, Grow and Sustain is a multi-year, core and flexible funding programme for feminist technology organising. It is open to initiatives, collectives, groups and organisations working to transform the relationship between technology, power, rights and social justice. SGS 3.0 is the third cycle of the programme. The first cycle was launched in 2022, and the latest call incorporates lessons collected through the earlier SGS 1.0 and SGS 2.0 cycles. The programme recognises that feminist technology organising is an emerging and diverse field. Some groups may be exploring feminist technology for the first time, while others may have developed tested strategies, regional networks or long-standing roles within the wider movement. For this reason, SGS 3.0 offers three funding levels that correspond to different stages of organising. SGS 3.0 Funding Levels 1. Seed: USD 10,000 to USD 20,000 Seed funding is intended to support emerging feminist technology collectives and initiatives. It may also support established activist groups that want to explore a feminist technology dimension within their existing work. This level may be appropriate for groups that are: Developing a new or emerging feminist technology idea; Engaging with technology as a field of activism for the first time; Forming a new collective or community initiative; Testing an early strategy or organising model; Adding a feminist technology dimension to established social-justice work; or Building initial relationships, knowledge or community participation around a technology-related issue. Seed funding recognises that new movements and ideas require resources before they can demonstrate large-scale results. Applicants do not need to present themselves as mature institutions if their work is genuinely at an emerging stage. 2. Grow: USD 20,000 to USD 50,000 Grow funding supports groups and initiatives that have been working together for at least two years, whether formally or informally. This level is intended for organisations seeking to deepen or expand their: Networks and partnerships; Communities and constituencies; Organising strategies; Existing activities or programmes; Geographic reach; Advocacy efforts; Feminist technology knowledge; or Engagement with new communities. A Grow applicant should be able to demonstrate that the group has already worked collectively and that it now has tested activities, strategies or relationships that can be expanded or strengthened. Formal legal registration is not necessarily required. The important consideration is whether the group has been organising together for at least two years and has an established body of work that it wants to deepen or expand. 3. Sustain: USD 50,000 to USD 100,000 Sustain funding is intended for established anchors within the feminist technology movement. Numun Fund uses the term “anchors” for organisations that lead and support local or regional processes alongside other feminist technology organisations, groups, collectives and activists. Sustain funding is intended to help these groups: Continue and strengthen their core strategies; Respond to changing political, technological or social conditions; Adapt their organising to emerging challenges; Maintain their role within local or regional movements; Support networks of activists and organisations; Address internal organising requirements; and Develop strategies for long-term sustainability. Applicants should choose the funding level that honestly reflects the maturity and purpose of their work. The preliminary eligibility assessment also recommends a funding level based on the applicant’s responses. Who Can Apply for SGS 3.0? SGS 3.0 supports collective organising led by communities whose realities, concerns and priorities are represented through the proposed work. Applicants may include: Legally registered organisations; Unregistered groups; Formally organised collectives; Informal initiatives; Online-only initiatives and web-based projects; Emerging feminist technology collectives; Established feminist or women-led organisations; Women-led programmes operating within larger human-rights organisations; Feminist programmes within digital-rights organisations; and Experienced organisations serving as local or regional movement anchors. Applicants can be new, emerging, established or experienced. The programme does not require every applicant to have the same institutional structure or level of development. However, every applicant must consist of at least two people. Applications from individuals are not supported. The official eligibility form asks whether the initiative is led by women in all their diversity. It explains this as women holding the majority of decision-making positions and occupying the principal leadership roles, whether those roles are held individually or shared. The fund’s understanding of women includes, among others: Trans women; Cisgender women; Non-binary people; Young and older women; Women with disabilities; Migrant and refugee women; Queer people; Afro-descendant women; and Women belonging to religious, linguistic or ethnic minorities. Feminist technology initiatives led by cisgender, heterosexual men are specifically listed among the forms of organising that the fund does not support. Eligible Regions and Communities SGS 3.0 prioritises organising and leadership located in the Larger Majority World. Numun Fund uses this concept in both a geographic and political sense to recognise the effects of colonialism, exploitation and historical inequality in the distribution of global resources. Eligible regions and communities include: West, Central, East and Southern Africa; Southeast Asia; South Asia; East Asia; West Asia and North Africa; Arabic-speaking countries; Latin America; The Caribbean; Pacific Island countries and communities; Eastern Europe; Central Asia; and Indigenous and migrant communities based anywhere in the world. Pakistan is included because it is located in South Asia. However, location alone does not establish eligibility. A Pakistan-based applicant would still need to satisfy the programme’s feminist technology, collective leadership, community connection and social-change requirements. Groups based in North America, Western Europe, Australia or New Zealand are generally not prioritised. An exception may apply where the group is led by Indigenous or migrant communities. Numun Fund also recognises that geographic and political identities do not always fit into simple regional categories. A group that believes it aligns with the fund’s stated politics and objectives but does not feel adequately represented by the listed regions may still apply. It should explain its circumstances and reasons in the additional-comments section. Essential Eligibility Requirements A competitive and eligible applicant should be able to demonstrate the following: Feminist technology is central to the work Technology cannot simply be an incidental tool used to manage an unrelated programme. It must be a key part of the initiative’s activism, advocacy, organising or approach to social change. Gender and sexuality are central to the analysis The eligibility assessment asks whether gender and sexuality are central to the applicant’s analysis of power, strategies and approach. Applicants should be able to explain how technological systems affect gendered power, rights, safety, participation or access. The applicant works collectively The programme funds groups and collective organising rather than individuals. A group must have at least two people. Women hold substantive leadership Leadership should not be symbolic. Women in all their diversity should hold the majority of decision-making roles and occupy the principal leadership positions. The work is community-led The initiative should be led by the communities whose realities and priorities it seeks to address or represent. Projects designed externally without meaningful community leadership are unlikely to align with the programme. The primary objective is social change The official eligibility check asks applicants to identify their primary strategy as social change rather than for-profit services, political or religious affiliation, or detached academic research. The work reaches historically marginalised communities Applicants should comprise, serve or connect with communities historically subjected to discrimination, oppression, exploitation or exclusion. These may include: Indigenous communities; Women and girls; Afro-descendant communities; Migrants; Refugees; LBTQI+ communities; Young people; People with disabilities; Women living in rural communities; Sex workers; Marginalised ethnic communities; Marginalised religious communities; and Linguistic minorities. What Does Feminist Technology Mean? Numun Fund does not impose one universal definition of feminist technology. It recognises that every context and movement may understand and experience technology differently. The central principle is the shifting of power. A feminist approach treats technology as a site of activism where political, economic and social systems can be reproduced, challenged or transformed. It asks who designs technology, who controls it, who benefits from it, who is harmed by it and whose knowledge is excluded. For SGS 3.0, feminist technology can be understood through four connected dimensions. 1. Analysis of Power Feminist technology uses feminist analysis to examine power structures and systems of oppression within digital technologies and science. This may include examining how technology interacts with: Patriarchy; Colonialism; Racism; Capitalism; Gender inequality; Economic exclusion; Surveillance; Data extraction; and Unequal access to knowledge and decision-making. The work should not stop at identifying problems. It should propose alternatives, responses, strategies or solutions that shift power towards affected communities. 2. Community Leadership Feminist technology centres communities that have historically been excluded, oppressed or discriminated against and that are often disproportionately affected by developments in science and technology. This means communities should not be treated merely as research subjects, beneficiaries or end users. They should participate in defining the problem, determining priorities, shaping strategies and leading the work. 3. Technology, Rights and Social-Justice Issues Eligible work may address a wide range of issues, including: Feminist digital safety; Bodily integrity and data privacy; Technology-facilitated gender-based violence; Freedom of expression online; Autonomous technology infrastructure for movement organising; Indigenous knowledge and the digital economy; Access to sexuality-related information and communities; Environmental justice and technology; Community-led engagement with the climate crisis and technology; Digital archives and memory projects; Gender and labour in the technology economy; Popular science education; Narrative power; Digital inclusion; Online organising spaces; and Majority World frameworks and alternative ways of imagining technology. This list is illustrative rather than exhaustive. Applicants may present other feminist technology priorities that are grounded in the realities of their communities. 4. Strategies for Activism The programme welcomes a wide range of organising strategies. These may include: Community-led research; Public campaigns; Technology design and development; Community building; Capacity development; Training; Knowledge sharing; Digital archiving; Artistic practices; Content creation; Policy advocacy; Convenings; Facilitation and holding spaces; Piloting alternative systems of social organising; Providing technology support to feminist activists; and Developing technology services connected directly to feminist movements. Research, software development or technology services may therefore be eligible when they are directly connected to movement organising and community leadership. Their eligibility depends on purpose, leadership and connection to social change rather than the activity alone. What SGS 3.0 Does Not Support Applicants should review the exclusions carefully before starting the application. Commercial technology providers For-profit developers or application creators that merely provide services to non-profit organisations are not supported when they have no direct connection to movement organising. Most Global North-based initiatives Groups based in Western Europe, North America, Australia or New Zealand are generally not eligible unless they are led by Indigenous or migrant communities. Global North-led projects without shared leadership Projects led from the Global North without direct peer partnership or shared leadership with Indigenous or migrant communities do not align with the fund’s objective of strengthening leadership in the Larger Majority World. Isolated technology initiatives Developers and technology service providers are not eligible when they lack a direct relationship with feminist, women’s-rights, digital-rights or social-justice movements. Cisgender heterosexual men-led organising Feminist technology initiatives led by cisgender, heterosexual men are not supported. The programme aims to strengthen the leadership of women in all their diversity. Political, governmental or religious dependence Groups structurally dependent on political parties, government agencies or religious institutions are not supported. Individual applications The programme does not fund individuals. Applicants must demonstrate collective organising involving at least two people. Detached academic research Academic research that is not directly connected to movements or led by the communities it examines is not supported. Research may still form part of an eligible strategy when it is movement-connected, community-led and directed towards feminist social change. How to Apply for Numun Fund SGS 3.0 The application process has two main stages. Step 1: Complete the Simple Eligibility Check Applicants must first complete the SGS 3.0 Simple Eligibility Check . The eligibility form asks about: The region where the applicant’s work is primarily based; Whether the group is part of an Indigenous, refugee or migrant community; Whether women hold the majority of leadership and decision-making roles; Whether information and communications technology or science is central to the activism; Whether gender and sexuality are central to the group’s analysis of power; Whether the primary strategy is social change; Whether the proposed work is new, expanding or part of an established core strategy; and The applicant’s likely Seed, Grow or Sustain level. Only one submission of the eligibility check is permitted. Applicants should therefore discuss their responses internally and verify their information before submitting it. If the assessment confirms eligibility, the applicant will be redirected to the full application form and given a recommended funding level. Applicants should immediately save the full application form or its link after completing the eligibility check. Step 2: Prepare the Full Application The full application asks applicants to describe: Their activism; Their existing work; Their communities and relationships; Their approach to feminist technology; Their organising history; The change they seek to create; and Their vision for the future. The application can be downloaded in plain-text format. This allows applicants with limited internet connectivity to work offline and supports people using screen readers. Groups can draft their responses collectively before returning to the online form. Applicants do not need to create an account on a separate platform to submit the application. The official SGS 3.0 application pack should be reviewed before submission. Application Deadline The final deadline is: Sunday, 6 September 2026 at 23:59 Anywhere on Earth, UTC−12. This deadline is equivalent to: Monday, 7 September 2026 at 4:59 p.m. Pakistan Standard Time. Applicants should not interpret the date only according to their local midnight. The Anywhere on Earth deadline is the controlling deadline published by Numun Fund. Early submission is strongly recommended because applicants must complete the eligibility check before accessing the full application. Selection Process and Timeline The SGS 3.0 grantmaking process has been informed by the Grantmaking Design Circle, an advisory group comprising activists and practitioners from feminist technology, human rights, women’s funds, intersectional feminism and social-justice movements. The selection process will also involve a community-led selection committee. This committee includes members of the Grantmaking Design Circle, organisations previously supported by Numun Fund, Numun Fund collaborators and activists from priority regions and movements. The expected timeline is: August 2026 Applications are open through the online form. Multilingual question-and-answer webinars will be held. Applicants can complete the eligibility assessment and full application. September 2026 Applications will be screened by the Numun Fund team. Applications that align with the published eligibility and priority criteria will be longlisted. October–November 2026 Longlisted applications will be reviewed by the community-led selection committee. Selection will be guided by the programme’s priorities and feminist technology criteria. December 2026 References and recommendations will be requested. Due-diligence procedures will be undertaken. Numun Fund may contact the applicant’s communities, partners or wider “constellation” as part of due diligence. January 2027 Application-status notifications are expected to be issued. Applicants should ensure that their named references, community partners and relevant collaborators understand the application and can credibly discuss the group’s work if contacted. Application Language and Accessibility English is currently the primary working language for the call and application process. Numun Fund recognises that many applicants will not speak English as their first language. Applications will be read with this understanding, and applicants should prioritise clarity and authenticity rather than attempting to use unnecessarily complicated language. The fund does not currently have the capacity to provide complete multilingual support throughout every stage of application, communication, review and due diligence. However, it may provide limited support through: Translation tools such as DeepL; Interpretation during selected webinars; Arabic interpretation; French interpretation; Hindi interpretation; Mandarin interpretation; Portuguese interpretation; Spanish interpretation; and Other languages where interpreters can be arranged. The downloadable plain-text application also supports screen readers and applicants with limited internet connectivity. SGS 3.0 Information Webinars Numun Fund has announced the following public online sessions: Wednesday, 19 August 2026, from 09:00 to 10:00 UTC, in English, with Portuguese, Hindi, French and Mandarin interpretation; Thursday, 20 August 2026, from 09:00 to 10:00 UTC, in Arabic, with English interpretation; and Thursday, 20 August 2026, from 14:00 to 15:00 UTC, in Spanish, with Portuguese, French and English interpretation. Registration links are available through the official SGS 3.0 page. The webinars will be treated as public spaces. Other participants may be able to see a person’s Zoom display name and profile photograph, and sessions may be recorded for internal documentation. Participants with security or privacy concerns should use a non-identifying display name and photograph. SGS 3.0 Signal Question-and-Answer Group A public SGS 3.0 Signal group will receive questions from Monday, 24 August to Wednesday, 26 August 2026. The Signal session will be conducted in English. Participants should be aware that their display name and profile photograph may be visible to other members of the public group. Anyone who does not want to be identified should adjust their Signal profile before joining. The official Signal-group link is available from the SGS 3.0 programme page. How to Prepare a Strong SGS 3.0 Application The following recommendations are based on the published eligibility criteria and are not additional official requirements. 1. Complete an internal eligibility review first Because the eligibility check can only be submitted once, applicants should review every question collectively before entering their final responses. 2. Demonstrate that technology is central Do not describe technology only as a communication tool used by the organisation. Explain how technology itself is connected to the power, rights, safety or social-justice issue being addressed. 3. Explain the feminist analysis clearly Show how gender and sexuality influence the problem, who holds power and how the proposed work seeks to change that situation. 4. Provide evidence of community leadership Identify who leads the group, who makes decisions and how affected communities determine the initiative’s priorities and strategies. 5. Select the correct funding level An emerging initiative should not claim to be a movement anchor merely to request a larger amount. The requested level should correspond to the group’s experience, existing work and intended strategy. 6. Describe relationships, not only activities Since the fund focuses on movement organising, applicants should explain their relationships with communities, activists, networks and partner organisations. 7. Prepare for due diligence Discuss the application with references and community partners in advance. The selection process may involve direct engagement with the applicant’s wider community and organisational network. 8. Use clear and accessible English Perfect English is not required. Applicants should use direct language, provide contextual explanations and avoid jargon that may obscure the importance of their work. 9. Submit before the deadline Completing the eligibility check does not constitute a full application. Applicants must obtain, complete and submit the full application form before the deadline. Where to Get Additional Support Applicants should first review the official programme page, application pack and frequently asked questions. Specific questions may be sent to grants@numun.fund using the subject line: SGS 3.0: Question Because Numun Fund operates with a small team, applicants should allow sufficient time for a response and should not wait until the final days before the deadline. Conclusion The Numun Fund Seed, Grow and Sustain 3.0 programme offers an important multi-year funding opportunity for women-led feminist technology groups across the Larger Majority World. With a total allocation of USD 1.75 million and individual funding ranging from USD 10,000 to USD 100,000, the programme can support initiatives at different stages—from emerging collectives developing their first feminist technology strategies to established organisations sustaining local and regional movements. The programme is not intended for individual applicants, conventional commercial technology providers or projects disconnected from feminist and social-justice movements. Strong applications will demonstrate collective leadership, community accountability, a clear feminist analysis of power and a meaningful connection between technology and social change. Eligible groups should complete the one-time eligibility assessment carefully, select the funding level that accurately reflects their stage of organising and submit the full application by Sunday, 6 September 2026 at 23:59 Anywhere on Earth. title: VFW-SVA Legislative Fellowship 2026–2027: Student Veterans Can Advocate on Capitol Hill with Travel Costs Covered
summary: Applications are now open for the 2026–2027 VFW-SVA Legislative Fellowship , an annual leadership and public-policy programme created by Student Veterans of America (SVA) in partnership with the Veterans of Foreign Wars of the United States (VFW) . Running from October 2026 through March 2027 , the fellowship gives selected student veterans the opportunity to develop practical advocacy skills, engage directly with policymakers, research issues affecting veterans and military-affiliated communities, and bring the perspectives of student veterans into national policy discussions. Fellows will work alongside SVA and VFW leaders on legislative priorities, participate in major advocacy activities, meet congressional leadership and committee staff, and travel to key events including SVA’s 19th Annual National Conference and the VFW Washington Conference. Importantly, the programme covers fellowship-related travel expenses for the required trips, including airfare, accommodation, local transportation and a per diem allowance. Applications opened on 1 August 2026 and must be submitted by 15 September 2026 . About the VFW-SVA Legislative Fellowship The VFW-SVA Legislative Fellowship is a collaborative initiative of Student Veterans of America and the Veterans of Foreign Wars. Established in 2014 , the programme was created to give student veterans a structured opportunity to translate their military experience, academic development and community engagement into meaningful policy advocacy. Rather than functioning solely as a classroom-based policy programme, the fellowship places participants directly into the world of veterans’ advocacy and government relations. Selected fellows learn how policy priorities are developed, communicated and advanced while gaining opportunities to interact with policymakers and national veteran-service leaders. The fellowship is particularly intended for student veterans who want to strengthen their ability to represent their peers and contribute to policy conversations affecting: Veterans Student veterans Active-duty service members Military-affiliated students Military families Survivors Veteran communities more broadly Programme Duration The 2026–2027 VFW-SVA Legislative Fellowship runs from October 2026 through March 2027 . During this period, fellows will participate in activities designed to build their knowledge of federal policy, leadership, advocacy and veterans’ affairs. Two major fellowship-related trips are planned: SVA 19th Annual NatCon Fellows will travel to Student Veterans of America’s 19th Annual National Conference in January 2027 . NatCon brings together student veterans, chapter leaders, universities, employers, partner organisations and other stakeholders connected to the student-veteran community. VFW Washington Conference Fellows will also attend the VFW Washington Conference in Washington, D.C., in March 2027 . This component gives participants an opportunity to engage directly in legislative advocacy and interact with congressional offices and policy leaders. What Fellows Will Do Selected participants will take part in a range of advocacy, leadership and policy-development activities. Work on a Legislative Priority Fellows will collaborate with VFW and SVA on a shared legislative priority relevant to veterans and military-affiliated communities. The programme provides an opportunity to understand how policy issues move from community concerns to research, advocacy strategies and engagement with government decision-makers. Engage with Congressional Leaders One of the programme’s central components is direct engagement with policymakers. Fellows may meet with: Members of Congress Congressional leadership Committee staff Legislative staff Veteran-policy advocates Other stakeholders working on veterans’ affairs These engagements can help fellows better understand how federal policymaking operates and how effective advocacy can influence policy outcomes. Participate in Team-Based Advocacy Participants will join VFW advocates from their states for advocacy meetings. This allows fellows to experience legislative engagement not simply as individuals, but as part of coordinated advocacy teams representing veteran interests. Develop Advocacy Skills The fellowship is designed to strengthen participants’ abilities to: Communicate policy priorities effectively Present compelling arguments Engage with policymakers Research veterans’ issues Build advocacy networks Translate lived experience into policy recommendations Represent veteran communities professionally Travel Costs Covered A particularly valuable feature of the fellowship is that required travel expenses associated with the two major programme trips are covered. The programme states that travel support includes: Airfare Hotel accommodation Local transportation to and from meetings Per diem allowance The covered trips include participation in the January 2027 SVA National Conference and the March 2027 VFW Washington Conference. Applicants should note that the supplied programme information describes travel support rather than a general fellowship stipend. Open to Students from All Academic Majors The fellowship is open to all majors . Applicants therefore do not necessarily need to study political science, international relations, public policy, law or another traditionally policy-oriented subject. A student veteran studying engineering, business, education, science, health, humanities, technology or another discipline may still be eligible if they satisfy the programme’s membership, enrolment and military-service requirements. The programme also notes that some participants may be able to receive college credit , although candidates should confirm any academic-credit arrangements with their own institution. Eligibility Requirements Applicants must satisfy several core requirements. To apply, candidates must: Be a current or eligible member of the Veterans of Foreign Wars Be enrolled at an accredited college or university during the fellowship Provide proof of current student enrolment Provide proof of military service The programme is specifically designed for student veterans who can bring both their military experience and current academic perspective into policy advocacy. Proof of Enrolment Applicants must demonstrate that they are enrolled at an accredited college or university during the fellowship period. Acceptable documentation may include: An unofficial academic transcript A class schedule A letter from the college or university confirming enrolment Applicants should make sure the document clearly demonstrates their current student status. Proof of Military Service Candidates must also provide evidence of military service. The programme identifies the DD214 as the preferred form of documentation. Applicants submitting a DD214 are specifically instructed to redact their Social Security Number before uploading the document . This is an important privacy and security step and should be completed before submission. Application Requirements Applying for the fellowship involves more than completing a short online form. Candidates are expected to demonstrate their interest in veteran advocacy, their leadership potential and their ability to communicate clearly. 1. Three-to-Five-Page Essay Applicants must prepare a 3–5 page essay addressing several areas. The essay should explain: Why veteran advocacy is important to the applicant How the applicant plans to use existing networks to advance advocacy goals How their current experience has shaped their approach to advocacy How participation in the fellowship would contribute to their development as a leader in the veteran community Candidates should use this essay to connect their military experience, student experience, community involvement and future aspirations. Specific examples will likely be more persuasive than general statements about leadership or public service. 2. Short Video Applicants must also submit a 30–60 second video . The video should explain: Why the applicant is interested in the fellowship What specifically attracts them to the programme How the fellowship connects with their personal and professional goals What they hope to gain What they hope to contribute as a fellow Because the video is short, applicants should plan a concise message rather than attempting to repeat the entire written essay. 3. Proof of Enrolment Applicants need to submit an unofficial transcript or another acceptable form of enrolment verification. 4. Resume A current resume must be included. Applicants should consider highlighting relevant experience such as: Military service Leadership Student-veteran organisation involvement Campus activities Community service Public-policy engagement Volunteer work Advocacy experience Professional experience 5. Proof of Military Service Military-service documentation is required, with the DD214 identified as the preferred document. Applicants should redact sensitive personal information where instructed. 6. Selection Interview Candidates who progress through the application process may participate in a virtual or telephone interview with the selection committee . Applicants should be prepared to discuss their interest in veteran advocacy, their leadership experience and what they hope to contribute to the fellowship. Key Dates Applicants should note the following schedule: Applications open: 1 August 2026 Application deadline: 15 September 2026 Fellowship duration: October 2026–March 2027 SVA 19th Annual NatCon: January 2027 VFW Washington Conference: March 2027 Applications must be submitted by 15 September 2026 . How to Apply Interested student veterans should submit their application through the official Student Veterans of America fellowship portal. APPLY HERE Applicants can also review the complete programme information HERE . Candidates should carefully review all instructions before uploading documents, particularly the requirements for the essay, video, enrolment verification and military-service documentation. Why the Fellowship Matters Student veterans occupy a distinctive position within higher education and the broader veteran community. They bring lived military experience into colleges and universities while simultaneously navigating academic, professional and civilian transitions. The VFW-SVA Legislative Fellowship creates a mechanism through which these experiences can inform policy conversations. Since its creation in 2014, the programme has helped student veterans develop experience in: Legislative advocacy Government relations Civic leadership Veterans policy Public service Nonprofit advocacy Former fellows have continued into leadership roles across public service, higher education, nonprofit advocacy and veterans’ services. The programme therefore provides not only a short-term advocacy experience but also an opportunity to build skills and professional networks relevant to longer-term careers in public policy and service. About Student Veterans of America Student Veterans of America is a nonprofit organisation focused on supporting and empowering student veterans. SVA operates through a network of more than 1,600 campus chapters across all 50 U.S. states and four countries , representing a community of nearly 600,000 student veterans . Its work includes programmes related to: Education Leadership development Advocacy Research Career development Campus support Professional networking The VFW-SVA Legislative Fellowship forms part of SVA’s wider effort to ensure student veterans have opportunities to develop leadership skills and participate meaningfully in public life. About the Veterans of Foreign Wars Founded in 1899 , the Veterans of Foreign Wars is one of the United States’ largest and longest-established veterans service organisations. Its membership consists of eligible veterans and military personnel from active-duty, Guard and Reserve forces. The organisation has more than 1.5 million VFW and Auxiliary members and over 6,000 Posts worldwide. The VFW works across areas including: Veterans services Legislative advocacy Military support Community service Veteran benefits Policy representation Its partnership with SVA helps connect student veterans with an established national advocacy network. Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application Candidates should begin preparing well before the September deadline because several different materials are required. Before submitting an application: Confirm that you are a current or eligible VFW member. Verify that you will remain enrolled at an accredited college or university during the fellowship. Prepare appropriate proof of enrolment. Locate your military-service documentation. Redact your Social Security Number from your DD214 before submission. Update your resume with relevant leadership, service and advocacy experience. Begin drafting the 3–5 page essay early. Use specific examples to demonstrate why veteran advocacy matters to you. Plan and rehearse the 30–60 second application video. Explain both what you hope to gain from the programme and what you can contribute. Submit before the final deadline rather than waiting until the last day. The strongest applications are likely to demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant’s experiences and their commitment to improving opportunities for veterans and military-affiliated communities. Conclusion The 2026–2027 VFW-SVA Legislative Fellowship provides student veterans with an opportunity to move beyond observing the policymaking process and participate directly in national veterans advocacy. Running from October 2026 through March 2027, the fellowship combines policy research, leadership development, congressional engagement, networking and hands-on legislative advocacy. Selected fellows will collaborate with Student Veterans of America and Veterans of Foreign Wars, attend the SVA National Conference, participate in the VFW Washington Conference and engage with congressional leaders and staff. Travel-related expenses for both major fellowship trips are covered, including airfare, lodging, local transportation and per diem. Applicants must be current or eligible VFW members and enrolled at an accredited college or university during the programme. Applications require an essay, a short video, enrolment verification, a resume and proof of military service. The application deadline is 15 September 2026 . For student veterans interested in public policy, civic leadership, government affairs and veteran advocacy, the fellowship offers a direct pathway to turn personal experience into meaningful policy engagement. title: ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 in Cambridge, UK: Fully Funded 10-Week AI Safety and Governance Research Programme
summary: Applications are now open for the ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 , an intensive 10-week research programme in Cambridge, United Kingdom, designed for talented individuals interested in advancing research on technical AI safety, AI governance and technical AI governance . The Winter 2027 ERA Fellowship will take place from 18 January to 26 March 2027 in Cambridge. Fellows will have the opportunity to work full-time on substantive research projects addressing some of the most important questions surrounding increasingly capable artificial intelligence systems. ERA seeks researchers, professionals, PhD students and other talented individuals from around the world who want to contribute to understanding and mitigating potentially catastrophic risks associated with frontier AI. Importantly, applicants do not necessarily need to come from a traditional artificial intelligence research background. ERA specifically encourages applications from early-career researchers, PhD students and working professionals, including people from fields such as computer science, engineering, law and related disciplines. Successful fellows will receive a competitive stipend , while ERA will also provide or cover key costs associated with participating in the programme, including lodging, transportation, visa support and meals during working hours . Applications for the Winter 2027 programme must be submitted by 13 September 2026 at 11:59 PM Anywhere on Earth (AoE) . About ERA and Its Mission ERA works to accelerate talent, advance research and strengthen organisations working to understand and reduce risks arising from increasingly capable frontier technologies, particularly advanced artificial intelligence. Its broader mission focuses on advancing scientific and policy breakthroughs that can help society mitigate risks from frontier technologies. In the context of artificial intelligence, ERA is concerned with complex challenges that could emerge as AI systems become increasingly capable and autonomous. These include questions surrounding the safe development and deployment of frontier AI, the preservation of meaningful human agency, governance mechanisms for powerful AI systems, and ways of preventing catastrophic outcomes associated with advanced artificial intelligence. ERA s work therefore brings together researchers working across both technical and governance disciplines. Rather than treating AI safety solely as a technical engineering problem or solely as a policy challenge, the programme supports work across the broader landscape of frontier AI safety and governance. What Is the ERA Fellowship Winter 2027? The ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 is a 10-week research and entrepreneurship programme based in Cambridge, UK. The programme will run from: Start date: 18 January 2027 End date: 26 March 2027 Duration: 10 weeks Location: Cambridge, United Kingdom Application deadline: 13 September 2026 at 11:59 PM Anywhere on Earth The fellowship is intended for researchers and entrepreneurs interested in understanding and mitigating catastrophic risks associated with frontier AI systems. During the programme, fellows work full-time on research questions they consider important while receiving mentorship, research management support and access to a broader community working on AI safety and governance. The fellowship also provides opportunities for projects that fall between established technical and policy research areas, making it particularly relevant for applicants interested in interdisciplinary approaches to advanced AI risks. ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 Research Tracks For the Winter 2027 cohort, ERA is accepting fellows across three main research tracks : AI Governance Technical AI Governance Technical AI Safety Applicants should carefully consider which track most closely matches their interests, experience and proposed research direction. Some questions on the application form only become available after an applicant selects a research track. 1. Technical AI Safety As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable and autonomous, understanding their behaviour and ensuring that humans can maintain meaningful oversight becomes more important. The Technical AI Safety track supports research addressing some of the central scientific and engineering problems associated with frontier AI safety. Research areas supported under this track can include: AI evaluations Interpretability Robustness AI alignment AI control Monitoring model behaviour Measuring potentially dangerous capabilities Eliciting capabilities from advanced AI systems Understanding the internal mechanisms of AI models Developing robust safeguards Controlling systems whose objectives may not be completely aligned with those of their operators These areas address difficult questions about how advanced AI behaves, how dangerous capabilities can be identified and measured, and how powerful systems can remain subject to meaningful human oversight. Fellows interested in machine learning, computer science, AI engineering, interpretability, alignment or related technical disciplines may find this track particularly relevant. 2. AI Governance The AI Governance track focuses on the institutions, policies, regulatory mechanisms and international arrangements that may be necessary as frontier artificial intelligence becomes increasingly powerful. As AI capabilities grow, decisions surrounding how advanced AI systems are developed, deployed and governed may have significant consequences. Effective AI governance therefore requires institutions capable of understanding rapidly evolving risks, developing credible rules and safeguards, and coordinating across national borders where risks and incentives affect multiple jurisdictions. ERA supports governance research in areas including: International cooperation on advanced AI AI regulatory tools Regulatory design and implementation Frontier AI safety frameworks Corporate governance Governance and accountability within frontier AI companies International coordination Institutional capacity for governing advanced AI systems This track may be especially relevant to researchers and professionals with backgrounds in areas such as law, public policy, international relations, economics, political science, governance and related fields. However, ERA does not restrict applications to these backgrounds. 3. Technical AI Governance Technical AI Governance, sometimes described as TechGov, operates at the intersection of technology and public governance. As frontier AI systems become increasingly capable, effective regulation may depend heavily on governments and institutions having access to reliable technical information and infrastructure. For example, regulators may need mechanisms for determining whether an AI system has crossed a particular capability or risk threshold. Policymakers may also need reliable methods for monitoring deployed AI systems or verifying whether organisations are complying with particular requirements. Technical AI governance explores how the technical foundations of artificial intelligence can make governance more informed, precise and enforceable. Research areas can include: Compute governance AI auditing Monitoring Hardware-enabled verification Technical standards Risk-relevant AI capability thresholds Verification mechanisms Privacy-preserving verification Technical infrastructure supporting AI regulation Projects may investigate questions such as how regulators could identify systems that exceed risk-relevant thresholds or how hardware and computing providers could facilitate effective verification while preserving privacy. This makes the track particularly relevant for people interested in combining technical knowledge with governance, regulation or policy. What Will ERA Fellows Do? One of the central components of the fellowship is the development of a substantive research project. During the 10-week programme, fellows work on their research with support from experienced mentors. ERA s mentor and institutional network extends across government, academia and industry and includes researchers connected with organisations and institutions such as the University of Cambridge, UK AI Security Institute, Centre for the Governance of AI, RAND Corporation, Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic , among others. The fellowship is designed to give participants significant scope to develop research addressing important questions within their chosen area. In addition to mentorship, fellows receive dedicated research management support and opportunities to discuss their research with other fellows and members of the Cambridge research community. Build a Substantive AI Research Portfolio A major objective of the ERA Fellowship is helping participants develop meaningful research experience and produce substantive work. Rather than simply attending lectures or seminars, fellows spend the programme actively developing a research project. The programme provides: Approximately 10 weeks of dedicated research time Experienced mentorship Research management support Access to a generous computing budget Interaction with other researchers and fellows Opportunities to engage with the University of Cambridge community Exposure to both technical AI safety and AI governance researchers This environment can be particularly valuable for individuals seeking to transition into AI safety or governance research or deepen an existing research portfolio. Professional Development and Long-Term Career Impact ERA states that it invests deeply in both the professional development and long-term impact of its fellows. Its support is built around individual research projects, high-touch mentorship and career support throughout the programme. The goal extends beyond helping fellows complete a single research project. ERA aims to help participants develop into researchers, entrepreneurs and policymakers who can contribute to shaping the future of advanced artificial intelligence. The fellowship can therefore provide participants with opportunities to: Develop specialised research expertise Build a substantive research portfolio Receive feedback from experienced researchers Explore career paths in AI safety and governance Connect with research organisations Develop professional relationships across academia, government and industry Become part of ERA s broader alumni and professional network Join a Global Network of ERA Alumni ERA reports having a network of more than 200 alumni . Its alumni have gone on to work at or become associated with a wide range of influential organisations spanning government, academia, AI research, public policy and nonprofit research. Organisations listed by ERA as workplaces of its alumni include: UK AI Security Institute European AI Office Center for AI Standards and Innovation RAND Corporation Centre for the Governance of AI Centre for AI Safety Future of Life Institute Machine Intelligence Research Institute Institute for AI Policy Strategy FAR AI Institute for Law AI Center for Strategic and International Studies METR Apollo Research Geodesic Research Constellation Institute Safe AI Forum Anthropic Google DeepMind Microsoft SaferAI MIT University of Cambridge SecureBio Amodo Design Stanford University The breadth of this network demonstrates the range of professional directions participants may explore following the fellowship. Participation in the programme does not, of course, guarantee employment with any of these organisations. More Than 30 Events During the Fellowship The ERA Fellowship is not limited to individual research. ERA states that it typically hosts more than 30 events throughout the fellowship period in Cambridge. These events provide additional opportunities for participants to engage with researchers, experts, professionals and other members of the AI safety community. The combination of independent research, structured mentorship and community events is designed to create an environment in which fellows can rapidly develop both their research and professional networks. Build Lasting Connections in Cambridge The fellowship also places considerable emphasis on community. Over approximately two and a half months, participants work alongside other fellows, full-time researchers and members of Cambridge s wider AI safety community. ERA has a dedicated Community Health Manager who organises weekly community health activities intended to strengthen social connections between fellows and the wider Cambridge community. ERA notes that many former participants remain connected years after completing their fellowships. For applicants seeking not only research experience but also sustained relationships with others working on advanced AI safety and governance, this community component may be an important feature of the programme. ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 Financial Support and Benefits The fellowship provides substantial financial and practical support intended to enable selected participants to spend the full programme working on their research in Cambridge. ERA states that fellows receive a competitive or generous stipend . In addition, support includes: Fellowship stipend Lodging for the duration of the fellowship Transportation support Visa expense support Meals during working hours Research management support High-touch mentorship Access to a generous compute budget Career support Access to ERA s wider professional and institutional network Participation in programme events and community activities This support can significantly reduce the financial and logistical barriers associated with relocating to Cambridge for the 10-week programme. International Applicants and Visa Sponsorship The ERA Fellowship welcomes talented applicants from around the world. ERA can provide visa sponsorship and visa-related expense support for fellows who require permission to travel to and participate in the programme in the United Kingdom. However, international applicants should pay particular attention to the programme s passport requirements. Applicants requiring visa sponsorship must ensure that their passport: Has at least one blank page available for the visa vignette; and Is valid until at least 26 September 2027 . Anyone whose passport does not meet these requirements is advised to begin the renewal process as soon as possible because passport renewal can take time. Who Is Encouraged to Apply? ERA states that it welcomes talented individuals from around the world and at any career stage who are motivated to contribute to AI safety and governance research. Applicants should not automatically exclude themselves because they believe they lack the conventional background for an AI fellowship. ERA explicitly encourages people to apply even when they are uncertain whether they satisfy every criterion or feel they do not have the right background. The programme is particularly interested in hearing from: Early-career researchers PhD students Working professionals People with backgrounds in computer science Engineers Legal professionals and researchers Individuals from related disciplines People interested in AI safety and governance who may come from other relevant backgrounds ERA makes clear that this list is non-exhaustive . Therefore, applicants from other academic or professional backgrounds who believe they can meaningfully contribute to the fellowship s mission are encouraged to submit an application. APPLY NOW Do You Need to Be an Established AI Researcher? Not necessarily. One particularly important aspect of the Winter 2027 application guidance is ERA s encouragement for people to apply even if they are uncertain whether they meet every criterion. The organisation is specifically interested in early-career researchers, PhD students and working professionals. That means applicants should evaluate their potential contribution based not only on whether they already have an established AI research career, but also on their relevant skills, research potential, professional experience, intellectual interests and motivation to address risks from advanced AI. Applicants should nevertheless carefully review ERA s research priorities before applying so that they understand the kinds of projects the programme seeks to support. Read ERA s Research Before Applying Prospective applicants are strongly advised to familiarise themselves with ERA s work before completing the application. ERA particularly recommends reviewing its: Website Past Research AI Risk materials General applicant guidance from previous application cycles Doing this should help applicants understand the types of research questions and approaches that align with the fellowship s mission. Candidates should also carefully consider the differences between AI Governance, Technical AI Governance and Technical AI Safety before choosing a track. ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 Application Process The initial stage of the application process primarily consists of short essay questions . ERA estimates that this stage should take approximately two hours to complete. Applicants are encouraged to prioritise the substance of their answers rather than spending excessive time polishing the writing. Applications will be assessed on a rolling basis . Applicants who successfully progress beyond the initial stage will be invited to complete two interviews . The general process therefore consists of: Review ERA s website, research and AI risk materials. Consider which of the three research tracks best matches your interests. Complete the online application form. Answer the required short essay questions. Submit the application before the deadline. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis. Candidates who progress will be invited to two interviews. Successful candidates will proceed toward participation in the Winter 2027 fellowship. Because applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, prospective applicants may wish to prepare and submit their application without unnecessarily waiting until the final deadline. Important Warning About AI Use in the Application Applicants should pay very close attention to ERA s academic integrity policy. ERA explicitly prohibits the use of AI tools to generate or refine written application responses. According to the application guidance, all written responses must be entirely the applicant s own work and should reflect their personal experiences, reasoning and insights. External assistance is prohibited, including: Using AI tools to generate answers Using AI tools to refine application responses Having other individuals help produce responses Other forms of external assistance with written answers ERA warns that applicants may be disqualified if it determines that their responses are not exclusively their own work. Applicants should therefore complete all application essay questions independently and comply fully with ERA s academic integrity requirements. Important Application Form Information Applicants should also be aware of two practical details when completing the form. First, some application questions only appear after selecting a research track . Applicants should therefore make sure they have selected their intended track and completed all questions associated with it before submitting. Second, the application form does not send confirmation emails after submission . Applicants should not assume that the absence of a confirmation email means their submission was unsuccessful. ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 Application Deadline The deadline for the Winter 2027 ERA Fellowship is: 13 September 2026 at 11:59 PM Anywhere on Earth (AoE). Applications submitted after the deadline may not be considered, so prospective candidates should plan accordingly. The programme itself will run from 18 January to 26 March 2027 in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Q A Session for Prospective Applicants ERA is also offering a Q A session for individuals who have questions about the fellowship or application process. Prospective candidates can register their interest through the registration option provided by ERA. Before contacting the organisation directly with questions, applicants are encouraged to read the FAQ on ERA s website. If their question remains unanswered after reviewing the FAQ, the fellowship team can be contacted at hello@erafellowship.org . Other ERA Programmes ERA has developed a broader portfolio of programmes addressing risks from frontier technologies. These include: ERA An intensive fellowship supporting researchers working on technical AI safety and AI governance. The next cycle is Winter 2027, with applications currently open. AI×Bio A programme bringing together machine learning, biology, public health and policy to reduce extreme biological risks. ERA has also indicated that an additional AI×Biosecurity Fellowship is planned for the same 18 January to 26 March 2027 period, with applications to be launched separately. Frontier AI Security Residency A project-led residency focused on areas including cybersecurity, hardware security, model protection and technical verification. Technical AI Governance Forum A programme convening technical and policy leaders to develop technical approaches and roadmaps for governing frontier AI. Together, these programmes reflect ERA s broader focus on developing talent, research and institutions capable of responding to challenges associated with transformative technologies. Why the ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 Could Be an Important Opportunity The ERA Fellowship offers an unusual combination of dedicated research time, mentorship, financial support, interdisciplinary collaboration and access to an established AI safety and governance community. Selected fellows are given approximately 10 weeks to focus intensively on a substantive research project while receiving support from experienced researchers. Several aspects make the programme particularly notable: It accepts applicants from around the world. Applicants can be at different career stages. ERA explicitly encourages candidates to apply even if they are uncertain about meeting every criterion. It supports technical and policy-oriented research. It provides a stipend and significant practical support. Visa-related costs and travel support are available. Lodging is covered for the programme duration. Fellows receive mentorship and research management support. Technical researchers can access a generous compute budget. Fellows join a community connected to major organisations across AI research, policy, academia and government. Participants can build a substantive research portfolio over an intensive 10-week period. For candidates who want to build a career addressing risks from increasingly capable artificial intelligence, the fellowship provides an opportunity to devote substantial time to research while developing professional connections in Cambridge. Key Dates and Details at a Glance Programme: ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 Location: Cambridge, United Kingdom Duration: 10 weeks Programme dates: 18 January–26 March 2027 Application status: Open Application deadline: 13 September 2026, 11:59 PM Anywhere on Earth (AoE) Research tracks: AI Governance, Technical AI Governance and Technical AI Safety Financial support: Competitive/generous stipend Accommodation: Covered for the fellowship duration Travel support: Available Visa support: Available Meals: Provided during working hours Selection process: Initial application followed by two interviews for progressing candidates Estimated initial application time: Approximately two hours Application review: Rolling basis Location requirement: Fellows participate in Cambridge, UK International applications: Welcomed Conclusion The ERA Fellowship Winter 2027 in Cambridge, UK provides an intensive opportunity for researchers, PhD students, professionals and other talented individuals interested in tackling some of the most consequential challenges associated with increasingly capable artificial intelligence. Running from 18 January to 26 March 2027 , the 10-week programme combines full-time research with high-touch mentorship, research management support, career development, community engagement and access to ERA s extensive network across academia, government, industry and the broader AI safety ecosystem. With three tracks covering AI Governance, Technical AI Governance and Technical AI Safety , the programme provides multiple pathways for applicants with technical, policy, legal, engineering, computer science and interdisciplinary backgrounds. ERA s willingness to consider applicants from around the world and at different career stages also makes the programme accessible to candidates who may not yet consider themselves established AI safety researchers. Successful fellows receive substantial practical support, including a stipend, lodging, transportation and visa expense support, meals during working hours and access to research resources such as a generous compute budget. Prospective applicants should carefully review ERA s website, past research and AI risk materials before submitting their applications. They should also remember that ERA strictly prohibits external assistance, including the use of AI tools, when writing or refining application responses. Most importantly, interested candidates should take note of the application deadline: 13 September 2026 at 11:59 PM Anywhere on Earth (AoE). Applicants who believe they could contribute to research aimed at understanding and mitigating catastrophic risks from frontier AI are encouraged by ERA to apply even if they are uncertain whether they meet every conventional criterion. title: Youth-Led Projects Competition 2026 to 2027: Win 3,000 CHF Funding to Build Flood and Drought Resilience in Your Community
summary: Young people are among the groups most affected by climate change, particularly as floods and droughts become increasingly frequent, severe, and unpredictable across the globe. Despite facing significant risks, young people possess the creativity, innovation, technical skills, and local knowledge needed to develop practical solutions that strengthen community resilience and support sustainable development. Recognizing the vital role of youth in addressing climate-related challenges, the Competition for Youth-Led Projects 2026–2027 is now accepting applications from young leaders with innovative ideas that improve resilience to floods and droughts. Following the success of previous editions, this international competition will award two youth-led projects with funding of 3,000 Swiss Francs (CHF) each . Selected project leaders will also receive expert guidance and mentorship throughout the implementation of their initiatives. If you are passionate about disaster risk reduction, climate adaptation, sustainable development, or community resilience, this is an excellent opportunity to transform your ideas into impactful action. About the Competition for Youth-Led Projects 2026–2027 The Competition for Youth-Led Projects is designed to encourage young people to take an active leadership role in developing practical, community-driven solutions that reduce the impacts of floods and droughts. The initiative recognizes that climate change is intensifying weather-related disasters worldwide and that youth involvement is essential for creating innovative, sustainable, and locally relevant responses. Rather than focusing only on awareness, the competition supports projects that can be implemented within communities and produce measurable results. Successful applicants will receive financial support and technical mentorship to help turn their ideas into real-world solutions over a nine-month implementation period. Why This Competition Matters Climate change is creating unprecedented challenges for communities around the world. Floods and droughts continue to affect: Food security Water availability Public health Livelihoods Agriculture Infrastructure Local economies Young people are particularly vulnerable because these disasters affect education, employment opportunities, health, and long-term economic security. However, youth also represent one of the greatest resources for climate innovation due to their: Creativity Digital skills Community engagement Scientific knowledge Ability to mobilize peers Passion for environmental sustainability This competition seeks to place youth at the center of climate resilience efforts while supporting the global Early Warnings for All (EW4All) initiative and broader disaster risk reduction strategies. Objectives of the Competition The Competition for Youth-Led Projects aims to achieve several important goals, including: Empower young people to design and lead practical climate resilience initiatives. Support disaster risk reduction, preparedness, and emergency response at the community level. Strengthen resilience against floods and droughts through locally driven solutions. Promote meaningful youth participation in climate action and environmental decision-making. Demonstrate the positive impact young leaders can make in protecting vulnerable communities. Encourage innovative approaches that can be expanded and replicated elsewhere. Funding Available The competition will fund two outstanding youth-led initiatives . Each selected project will receive: Funding of 3,000 CHF Expert mentoring throughout implementation Technical guidance from specialists in flood and drought resilience Recognition as a winning youth-led climate resilience initiative Opportunities to contribute to global climate adaptation efforts Project Implementation Period Awarded projects will be implemented over a maximum period of 9 months . During this time, project leaders will work closely with technical experts who will provide support, guidance, and feedback to maximize project impact. Eligibility Criteria Applicants must satisfy all mandatory eligibility requirements. Projects Must Be Youth-Led Projects must be designed and led by: Students Young professionals Young leaders aged 18–35 years Applicants must also demonstrate the active involvement and participation of young people below the age of 35 throughout the implementation process. Project Requirements Eligible projects should: Be practical and action-oriented. Have clearly defined objectives. Include a realistic implementation timeline. Clearly define the project s scope. Deliver measurable and tangible outcomes. Directly contribute to improving resilience against floods and droughts. Be completed within nine months. Demonstrate sustainability beyond the funding period. Show potential for scaling or replication in other communities. Innovation Requirements Projects should include innovative elements that improve resilience through new or creative approaches. Examples include: Combining Indigenous knowledge with scientific approaches. Developing innovative community engagement strategies. Introducing affordable climate adaptation solutions. Promoting strong participation and leadership by women. Applying technology to improve disaster preparedness. Creating locally adapted resilience models. What Makes a Strong Proposal? Successful proposals should demonstrate: A clearly identified community need. Practical and achievable objectives. Strong youth leadership. Community participation. Innovation. Sustainability. Scalability. Tangible outcomes. Realistic budgeting and planning. Language Options Applicants may submit proposals in either: English Spanish Only one proposal may be submitted per applicant. Submitting multiple applications or submitting in more than one language will result in disqualification. How to Apply Before submitting your proposal, applicants should carefully review the official Submission Guidelines available in both English and Spanish. After reviewing the guidelines: Complete the official submission form. Submit your proposal in either English or Spanish. Ensure your application is submitted only once. Verify that all required information has been completed before submission. Only proposals submitted through the official submission forms will be considered. APPLY HERE Application Deadline Deadline for submissions: 31 August 2026 Late submissions will not be accepted. Applicants are encouraged to prepare their proposals well in advance to avoid last-minute technical issues. Contact Information For questions regarding the competition or submission process, applicants may contact: Email: droughtmanagement@wmo.int Why You Should Apply This competition provides much more than financial support. It offers young innovators the opportunity to transform local ideas into meaningful climate action while gaining recognition and mentorship from experts working in disaster risk reduction and climate resilience. Whether your project focuses on community preparedness, sustainable agriculture, innovative water management, climate education, Indigenous knowledge, women s leadership, or nature-based solutions, this programme offers an ideal platform to demonstrate how youth-led initiatives can contribute to safer and more resilient communities. By participating, young leaders can strengthen their leadership skills, expand their professional networks, and contribute directly to global efforts aimed at reducing the impacts of floods and droughts. Visit HERE to learn more about the Youth-Led Projects Competition 2026 to 2027 Conclusion The Competition for Youth-Led Projects 2026–2027 represents an outstanding opportunity for young changemakers to transform innovative climate resilience ideas into real-world solutions. With funding of 3,000 CHF available for two outstanding projects, along with expert mentorship and international recognition, the programme empowers youth to play a leading role in disaster risk reduction and sustainable development. If you are a young leader passionate about climate action, community resilience, and disaster preparedness, this competition offers the resources and support needed to create lasting impact. Begin preparing your proposal today and submit your application before the 31 August 2026 deadline.
